title: Allocation rate limits cap the velocity of capital movement, not the total amount that can be allocated
content:
A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.1.1 describes the Rate Limiter as enforcing "constraints on controller operations to prevent rapid asset drainage and mitigate risks from compromised relayers or other attacks," implemented via `RateLimits` contracts. A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.1.2 gives the formula: `currentRateLimit = min(slope * (block.timestamp - lastUpdated) + lastAmount, maxAmount)`, where `maxAmount` and `slope` are governance-set and `lastAmount`/`lastUpdated` are internal state.

It then states plainly what the mechanism is *not*: "Rate limits set caps on the rate of allocation to a given Instance, **they do not act as a limit on the total amount that may be allocated to that Instance**."

This is a leaky-bucket allowance, and the distinction is the whole security argument. Total-exposure limits are a *risk* control, answering how much of a thing the system should own; rate limits are an *attack* control, answering how fast value can leave through a compromised path. An attacker with relayer access is bounded not by how much exists but by how much refills per unit time, which buys the window in which humans can respond.

The two parameters tune that window independently. A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.1.2.1 makes `maxAmount` a hard cap on the allowance at any instant — the largest single movement possible — while A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.1.2.2 makes `slope` the refill rate, determining sustained throughput. A low `maxAmount` with a fast `slope` permits high volume in small pieces; the reverse permits rare large moves.

Total exposure is governed elsewhere — by aggregate exposure limits (A.2.2.10.1.1.1.1.4) and by the Risk Capital and ALM frameworks — which is why the rate limiter can be tuned purely for containment.
description: A linearly refilling allowance — slope times elapsed time, capped at maxAmount — exists to prevent rapid drainage by compromised relayers rather than to bound total exposure.
